raw_model_deviations.claim_in_article:
Ring, ring. A call seemed to come from an AI agent. But as the conversation went on, the voice was not AI at all. It was a person.

Meta had run a test that caused exactly this surprise.
raw_model_deviations.issue: The article presents a caller’s mistaken impression and subsequent discovery of a human during a call as an event caused by Meta’s test. The Ledger verifies that humans handled some calls, but does not verify that a caller thought a call was AI or experienced this reveal.
raw_model_deviations.explanation: The human-handled calls are verified, but the caller’s belief, discovery, and resulting surprise are not; saying the test caused the surprise adds an unsupported causal event.
raw_model_deviations.qualifier_text: A call seemed to come from an AI agent; In some calls through Muse
same_fact_id_locations: We Thought It Was AI—But There Was a Person Inside Meta’s Muse
It was like someone took off an AI costume. Then a person stepped out.
### The hidden person behind the AI sign
A human stood behind the sign that said AI.

raw_model_deviations.claim_in_article: The test began without clearly telling users that contract workers would make the calls. A user might think the exchange was with AI, even though a person was involved.
raw_model_deviations.issue: The article attributes lack of disclosure and possible unawareness to users without retaining the Ledger’s internal-test scope: the human concierge feature was enabled for Meta employees. The Ledger does not establish that product users outside that test population were affected or unaware.
raw_model_deviations.explanation: The Ledger describes an employee test, whereas the article’s unqualified “users” broadens the affected group; “might” hedges the belief claim but does not establish that broader scope.
raw_model_deviations.qualifier_text: A user might think the exchange was with AI
same_fact_id_locations: A Meta executive admitted the mistake. The test had begun without clearly telling users.
